nodes.rationale: Two POSSIBLE user flows sketched by the RFC, neither shipped: `graphify . --summarize-nodes` under Option A, or an explicit `graphify summarize` command under Option B. Whether generation happens during graph creation or only through an explicit command is an unresolved question.

nodes.label: Suggested first implementation (5 steps)
nodes.rationale: Once storage is chosen: (1) add deterministic file-level summary generation, (2) store summaries using the selected option, (3) surface them in `graphify explain`, (4) surface them in `graphify serve` / MCP node lookup, (5) add tests for default behavior, generated summaries, missing summaries, and bounded summary length.

nodes.label: Follow-up: opt-in LLM-generated summaries
nodes.rationale: Follow-up idea, explicitly outside the first version: add opt-in LLM-generated summaries with explicit provider/backend selection. Kept opt-in so the default stays offline and deterministic.

nodes.label: Follow-up: extend to class/module-level nodes
nodes.rationale: Follow-up idea, conditional on evidence: extend summaries to class or module-level nodes IF file-level summaries prove useful. Not part of the first version.

nodes.label: Follow-up: summaries in query results under a budget
nodes.rationale: Follow-up idea: allow `graphify query` to include summaries for returned nodes under a budget — a third consumption surface beyond explain and serve/MCP, gated so it cannot blow up result size.

nodes.label: Follow-up: cache/freshness metadata
nodes.rationale: Follow-up idea, conditional on the storage choice: add cache/freshness metadata IF summaries are generated separately from the main graph — i.e. it is the answer to the synchronization problem the sidecar option introduces.

nodes.label: Open question 1: one artifact or a sidecar?
nodes.rationale: Unresolved question for maintainers and users: should graphify prefer one artifact (`graph.json`) or keep generated text in a sidecar? This is the decision the whole RFC is blocked on — summaries are not to be emitted by default until it is settled.

nodes.label: Open question 2: generate at build time or on command?
nodes.rationale: Unresolved question: should deterministic file-level summaries be generated during graph creation, or only through an explicit command such as `graphify summarize`?

nodes.label: Open question 3: summary or synopsis?
nodes.rationale: Unresolved naming question: is `summary` the right term, or would `synopsis` better communicate a short, bounded description? The field name in every example is therefore provisional.

nodes.label: Open question 4: length budget for large repositories
nodes.rationale: Unresolved question: what summary length budget would be acceptable for large repositories? The '200-300 characters' figure in the constraints is offered only as an example, which is why the budget is still being asked about.

nodes.label: graphify Security Policy
nodes.rationale: graphify's SECURITY.md declares which versions are supported, how to report a vulnerability privately, the project's security model as a local development tool, its threat surface with per-vector mitigations, and an explicit list of what graphify does NOT do.

nodes.label: Supported versions: 0.3.x only
nodes.rationale: The support table states 0.3.x is supported and anything below 0.3 is not. This is a stated CEILING on the version range receiving security fixes; the document names no exception or override for older lines.

nodes.label: Private vulnerability reporting
nodes.rationale: Security issues must NOT be filed as public GitHub issues; they go through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting or direct email to the maintainer, including a description, reproduction steps, potential impact, and a suggested fix if any.

nodes.label: 48-hour acknowledgement target
nodes.rationale: The maintainers state they will acknowledge receipt of a vulnerability report within 48 hours. It is an aim stated in the policy, not a contractual guarantee, and no escalation path is documented if it is missed.

nodes.label: 7-day fix target for critical issues
nodes.rationale: The policy aims to release a fix within 7 days for CRITICAL issues. The 7-day figure is CONDITIONED on criticality — non-critical issues carry no stated turnaround at all.

nodes.label: Security model: local development tool
nodes.rationale: graphify is positioned as a local development tool that runs as a Claude Code skill and optionally as a local MCP stdio server. The whole threat model rests on that locality assumption.

nodes.label: No network calls during graph analysis
nodes.rationale: graphify makes no network calls during graph analysis; the only network activity is during `ingest`, an explicit URL fetch initiated by the user. The claim is CONDITIONED on the analysis phase, not on the tool as a whole.

nodes.label: Threat surface table
nodes.rationale: SECURITY.md enumerates ten attack vectors against graphify and pairs each with the concrete function or code construct that mitigates it, making the mitigation a named symbol rather than a claim.

nodes.label: Vector: SSRF via URL fetch
nodes.rationale: Because graphify fetches user-supplied URLs during ingest, server-side request forgery against private networks or cloud metadata endpoints is a named vector in the threat surface.

nodes.label: security.validate_url()
nodes.rationale: `security.validate_url()` allows only the `http` and `https` schemes, blocks private, loopback and link-local IPs, and blocks cloud metadata endpoints. It is an allowlist on scheme and a blocklist on destination address.

nodes.label: Redirect targets are re-validated
nodes.rationale: URL validation is not applied only to the originally supplied URL: redirect targets are re-validated, closing the classic SSRF bypass where a public URL 302s to a private or metadata address.

nodes.label: safe_fetch()
nodes.rationale: `safe_fetch()` is the single chokepoint every fetch path in graphify goes through, including tweet oEmbed. It streams responses, enforces a size ceiling, and raises on non-2xx status.

nodes.label: Tweet oEmbed routed through safe_fetch
nodes.rationale: The policy calls out that ALL fetch paths, explicitly including the tweet oEmbed path, go through `safe_fetch()` — naming the one path most likely to have been a side door.

nodes.label: Vector: oversized downloads
nodes.rationale: A remote server returning an unbounded response body is a named vector: without a ceiling, a fetch could exhaust memory or disk. Mitigated by streaming plus a hard abort threshold.

nodes.label: CAP: safe_fetch aborts at 50 MB
nodes.rationale: `safe_fetch()` streams the response and ABORTS at 50 MB. SECURITY.md states the figure flatly, with no condition attached and NO environment variable, flag, or config key documented anywhere in this file for raising or lowering it.

nodes.label: safe_fetch_text()
nodes.rationale: `safe_fetch_text()` is the text-returning sibling of `safe_fetch()` and carries its own, tighter size ceiling — the two caps are separate numbers, not one shared limit.

nodes.label: CAP: safe_fetch_text aborts at 10 MB
nodes.rationale: `safe_fetch_text()` aborts at 10 MB — one fifth of the 50 MB binary-fetch cap. Which ceiling applies is CONDITIONED on which function the caller used. No override environment variable is documented in SECURITY.md.

nodes.label: Non-2xx responses raise HTTPError
nodes.rationale: `safe_fetch()` raises `HTTPError` on non-2xx status codes so that error pages are never silently treated as content — a fetch that failed cannot enter the graph as text.

nodes.label: Vector: path traversal in the MCP server
nodes.rationale: The MCP server accepts a graph path from its caller, so an unconstrained path would let a client read files outside the project — path traversal is a named vector.

nodes.label: security.validate_graph_path()
nodes.rationale: `security.validate_graph_path()` RESOLVES paths (defeating `..` segments) and requires the result to be inside `graphify-out/`. It additionally requires the `graphify-out/` directory to exist, so a missing directory is a refusal rather than a permissive fallback.

nodes.label: Vector: XSS in graph HTML output
nodes.rationale: Node labels and edge titles derived from user-controlled source files are embedded into pyvis HTML output, so unescaped labels would be a cross-site-scripting vector in the rendered graph.

nodes.label: security.sanitize_label()
nodes.rationale: `security.sanitize_label()` strips control characters, caps label length, and HTML-escapes every node label and edge title before pyvis embeds them. The same function is reused on MCP text output, so it defends two different sinks.

nodes.label: CAP: labels truncated at 256 chars
nodes.rationale: `sanitize_label()` caps labels at 256 characters. This is a silent truncation ceiling on every node label and edge title that reaches HTML output or MCP text output; SECURITY.md documents no environment variable or flag to change it.

nodes.label: Vector: prompt injection via node labels
nodes.rationale: Node labels come from user-controlled source files and are returned to agents through MCP text output, so an unsanitised label could break the text format and inject instructions into the consuming agent.

nodes.label: Vector: prompt injection via source file content
nodes.rationale: During the semantic pass, source files are attacker-controlled text mixed directly into the LLM context. This is the hardest vector in the table and is tracked upstream as issue #1210.

nodes.label: Hash-stamped <untrusted_source> delimiter block
nodes.rationale: `_read_files()` in `llm.py` wraps every source file in a `<untrusted_source path=... sha256=...>` delimiter block. The sha256 stamp is what makes a forged closing tag detectable rather than merely discouraged.

nodes.label: System prompt declares the block inert data
nodes.rationale: The extraction system prompt instructs the model to treat the delimited block as inert data and never as instructions — the model-side half of the delimiter defense, and by nature advisory rather than enforced.

nodes.label: _neutralise_injection_sentinels()
nodes.rationale: `_neutralise_injection_sentinels()` defangs KNOWN chat-template and jailbreak tokens — `<|im_start|>`, `[INST]`, `<<SYS>>`, a forged `</untrusted_source>`, and similar — before insertion into the prompt. Its coverage is a blocklist of known tokens, so unknown sentinels are out of scope by construction.

nodes.label: CEILING: injection defense is table stakes, not impossibility
nodes.rationale: graphify states its own ceiling explicitly: the delimiter + system-prompt + sentinel-defanging stack is the table-stakes defense for issue #1210 and 'does not make injection impossible' — it only changes the cost from 'works on first try' to 'requires evasion'.

nodes.label: Vector: YAML frontmatter injection
nodes.rationale: User-controlled strings such as webpage titles and query questions are embedded into YAML frontmatter, where an unescaped quote or newline would let the value break out and forge additional frontmatter keys.

nodes.label: _yaml_str() escaping
nodes.rationale: `_yaml_str()` escapes backslashes, double quotes, and newlines before any user-controlled string (webpage title, query question) is embedded in YAML frontmatter.

nodes.label: Byte slices decoded with errors="replace"
nodes.rationale: All tree-sitter byte slices are decoded with `errors="replace"`, so a non-UTF-8 source file degrades gracefully — with replacement characters in the extracted text — instead of crashing extraction.

nodes.label: os.walk(followlinks=False) throughout detect.py
nodes.rationale: Symlink traversal is mitigated by passing `followlinks=False` explicitly to every `os.walk` in `detect.py`, so a symlink inside a scanned tree cannot pull the walker outside it.

nodes.label: Corrupted graph.json handled in _load_graph()
nodes.rationale: `_load_graph()` in `serve.py` wraps `json.JSONDecodeError` and prints a clear recovery message rather than crashing, so a truncated or corrupted `graph.json` yields a diagnosable failure instead of a stack trace.

nodes.label: No network listener by default (stdio transport)
nodes.rationale: graphify does not run a network listener by default: the MCP server's default transport is stdio, so nothing binds a port unless the operator opts in.

nodes.label: --transport http is opt-in and binds 127.0.0.1
nodes.rationale: `--transport http` is opt-in and documented in the README. Its loopback binding is a CONDITIONAL default, not a hard ceiling: it binds to `127.0.0.1` UNLESS `--host 0.0.0.0` is passed, which is the documented override that exposes the server to the network.

nodes.label: Does not execute code from source files
nodes.rationale: graphify never executes code from the source files it analyses — tree-sitter parses ASTs, and there is no eval or exec of ingested content.

nodes.label: No shell=True in any subprocess call
nodes.rationale: No subprocess call in graphify uses `shell=True`, eliminating shell-metacharacter injection through any argument graphify passes to a child process.

nodes.label: Does not store credentials or API keys
nodes.rationale: graphify stores no credentials or API keys, so there is no secret at rest for a compromised graph directory or a leaked artifact to disclose.

nodes.label: Optional network calls, enumerated
nodes.rationale: SECURITY.md enumerates the complete set of paths that can reach the network, so any observed traffic outside that list is a defect: only `ingest` fetches, while PDF extraction and watch mode are local-only.

nodes.label: ingest fetches user-provided URLs
nodes.rationale: The `ingest` subcommand fetches URLs EXPLICITLY provided by the user — it is the sole intentional network egress and the reason validate_url/safe_fetch exist.

nodes.label: PDF extraction is local-file only
nodes.rationale: PDF extraction reads local files only; pypdf makes no network calls, so ingesting a PDF cannot cause remote fetches of embedded references.

nodes.label: watch mode is local filesystem events only
nodes.rationale: watch mode consumes local filesystem events only; watchdog makes no network calls, so a long-running watcher adds no egress surface.

nodes.label: No override env var documented for any stated cap
nodes.rationale: SECURITY.md names three numeric ceilings (50 MB, 10 MB, 256 chars) and attaches NO environment variable, CLI flag, or config key to any of them. The file mentions exactly one documented override anywhere — `--host 0.0.0.0`, which loosens the HTTP transport's loopback binding — so silence here is the document's limit, not proof the caps are hard in the installed code.

nodes.label: graphify pipeline (/graphify)
nodes.rationale: The /graphify skill turns any folder of files (code, docs, papers, images, video) into a navigable knowledge graph with community detection and an honest audit trail, producing three outputs: interactive HTML, GraphRAG-ready JSON, and a plain-language GRAPH_REPORT.md. The runbook is an ordered sequence of numbered steps (0 through 9) and the instruction is explicit: 'Follow these steps in order. Do not skip steps.'

nodes.label: CLI/flag usage surface
nodes.rationale: The Usage block enumerates the whole invocation surface: a bare path or one/many GitHub URLs, --branch, --mode deep, --update, --directed, --whisper-model, --cluster-only, --no-viz, --html (a documented no-op since HTML is default), --svg, --graphml, --neo4j/--neo4j-push, --falkordb/--falkordb-push, --mcp, --watch, --wiki, --obsidian/--obsidian-dir, plus the subcommands add, query (with --dfs and --budget), path and explain.

nodes.label: --help prints Usage and stops
nodes.rationale: If the user invoked /graphify --help or -h with no other arguments, the agent must print the Usage section verbatim and stop: run no commands, do not detect files, do not default the path to '.'.

nodes.label: Fast path — existing graph answers questions
nodes.rationale: Before anything else the agent checks whether graphify-out/graph.json exists relative to the current working directory. If it does and the request is a natural-language question about the codebase (not an explicit rebuild via --update, --cluster-only, or a bare path/URL), Steps 1-5 are skipped entirely and `graphify query "<question>"` runs immediately — no detect, no corpus-size check, no asking the user to narrow.

nodes.label: Step 0 — GitHub clone and multi-path merge
nodes.rationale: Step 0 runs only when the path argument is one or more https://github.com/... URLs, or several local subfolders to merge; it clones and performs the cross-repo/monorepo merge (detail in references/github-and-merge.md) and then continues with the resolved local path. A plain local path skips this step.

nodes.label: Step 1 — ensure graphify is installed
nodes.rationale: Step 1 resolves the correct Python interpreter across uv tool, pipx, venv and system installs: try `uv tool run --from graphifyy python`, else read the shebang off the `graphify` binary and validate it can `import graphify`, else fall back to python3; if the import still fails it installs graphifyy via uv tool install or pip (with --break-system-packages as a last resort). If the import succeeds it prints nothing and moves straight to Step 2.

nodes.label: .graphify_python interpreter marker
nodes.rationale: Step 1 writes sys.executable to graphify-out/.graphify_python so the resolved interpreter persists across invocations. Every subsequent bash block must replace `python3` with `$(cat graphify-out/.graphify_python)` to use the correct interpreter.

nodes.label: .graphify_root scan-root marker
nodes.rationale: Step 1 also records the absolute scan root into graphify-out/.graphify_root so that a later bare `graphify update` (with no args) knows where to look. It is distinct from the project root/cwd used for chunk paths and Part C globbing (#1392).

nodes.label: Step 2 — detect files
nodes.rationale: Step 2 runs detect() over INPUT_PATH into graphify-out/.graphify_detect.json. The JSON must NOT be cat'd or printed — it is read silently and summarised as 'Corpus: X files · ~Y words' broken down by code/docs/papers/images/video, omitting any zero category. If total_files is 0 the run stops with 'No supported files found in [path].'

nodes.label: graphify.detect.detect()
nodes.rationale: `from graphify.detect import detect` — detect(Path(INPUT_PATH)) returns a JSON-serialisable dict carrying total_files, total_words, skipped_sensitive, an absolute scan_root, and a `files` map keyed by category (code, document, paper, image, video); in --update mode it also carries `all_files` for the full corpus while `files` holds the changed subset.

nodes.label: Corpus-size warning and narrow-to-subfolder prompt
nodes.rationale: If total_words > 2,000,000 OR total_files > 500 the agent shows the warning, then ranks the top 5 first-level subdirectories by file count — reading scan_root from the detect JSON, concatenating all file lists across every type, filtering out anything under scan_root + '/graphify-out/', and bucketing files with no subdirectory as '(root)'. It then asks which subfolder to run on and waits. If everything is in '(root)' it does not ask to narrow and instead suggests --no-cluster.

nodes.label: skipped_sensitive must be reported (#2106)
nodes.rationale: When detect returns a non-empty skipped_sensitive list, the agent reports the count and lists the skipped file names, so a wrongly-flagged source or doc is visible and can be renamed or moved (#2106).

nodes.label: Step 2.5 — video and audio transcription
nodes.rationale: Step 2.5 is skipped entirely when detect returned zero video files. Otherwise the video/audio is transcribed to text first (see references/transcribe.md, and --whisper-model to pick a larger Whisper model) and the transcripts are then treated as ordinary doc files in Step 3.

nodes.label: Step 3 — extract entities and relationships
nodes.rationale: Step 3 splits into structural extraction (deterministic, free) and semantic extraction (LLM, costs tokens), and the runbook requires them to run in parallel: dispatch all semantic subagents AND start AST extraction in the same message, then merge in Part C. Parallelising saves 5-15s on large corpora. Whether --mode deep was given must be tracked from the original invocation and passed as DEEP_MODE to every subagent.

nodes.label: No API key required — never block on one
nodes.rationale: 'graphify needs no API key. Never ask the user for one, and never block on one.' Code is extracted structurally by AST with no LLM and no key, so a code-only corpus skips semantic extraction entirely. graphify does not read ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, or any other provider key; prompting for or stopping on a missing key is explicitly a misread of the skill.

nodes.label: Optional Gemini semantic backend
nodes.rationale: If GEMINI_API_KEY or GOOGLE_API_KEY is already set, semantic extraction uses graphify.llm.extract_corpus_parallel(files, backend="gemini") instead of dispatching subagents; the default model is gemini-3-flash-preview, overridable via GRAPHIFY_GEMINI_MODEL or --model in headless CLI flows. If neither key is set the agent prints one tip line once and continues without waiting — the host agent itself becomes the LLM.

nodes.label: Host agent is the fallback LLM
nodes.rationale: With no Gemini key, semantic extraction falls to the running session itself. On a host that can dispatch subagents (e.g. Claude Code) they are dispatched as in Part B; on a CLI host that cannot, a code-only corpus writes the empty semantic file and continues, while a docs/papers/images corpus is either given a Gemini key or extracted inline — in no case is ANTHROPIC_API_KEY prompted for.

nodes.label: Part A — structural (AST) extraction
nodes.rationale: Part A expands the detect JSON's `code` list (recursing into directories with collect_files) and runs extract(code_files, cache_root=Path(INPUT_PATH)) into graphify-out/.graphify_ast.json, printing 'AST: N nodes, M edges'. When there are no code files it still writes an empty {nodes,edges,input_tokens,output_tokens} document so downstream merges have their input.

nodes.label: graphify.extract.collect_files / extract
nodes.rationale: `from graphify.extract import collect_files, extract` — collect_files(Path) enumerates code files under a directory, and extract(code_files, cache_root=...) returns a dict with 'nodes' and 'edges' produced deterministically by AST parsing, with no LLM call and therefore no token cost.

nodes.label: Part B — semantic extraction via parallel subagents
nodes.rationale: Part B is the LLM pass over docs, papers and images. Using the Agent tool is MANDATORY — reading the files one-by-one is forbidden and 5-10x slower. Before dispatching, the agent prints a timing estimate computed from total_words and file counts: agents ≈ ceil(uncached_non_code_files / 22), time ≈ 45s per parallel batch.

nodes.label: Fast-path empty .graphify_semantic.json
nodes.rationale: If detection found zero docs, papers and images (a code-only corpus), Part B is skipped — but an empty {nodes,edges,hyperedges,input_tokens,output_tokens} must first be written to graphify-out/.graphify_semantic.json, because Part C's merge reads that file unconditionally and a code-only run would otherwise hit FileNotFoundError.

nodes.label: Step B0 — check the extraction cache first
nodes.rationale: Before any subagent is dispatched, B0 calls check_semantic_cache to split files into cached hits and an uncached list, writing hits to .graphify_cached.json and the remainder to .graphify_uncached.txt, and printing 'Cache: N files hit, M files need extraction'. When there are no hits it DELETES any leftover .graphify_cached.json so Part C can never merge a stale one (#1392). If every file is cached, the run skips straight to Part C.

nodes.label: graphify.cache.check_semantic_cache
nodes.rationale: check_semantic_cache(all_files, root=INPUT_PATH, prompt_file=SPEC_PATH) returns a four-tuple (cached_nodes, cached_edges, cached_hyperedges, uncached) — the replayable cached graph fragments plus the list of files that still need extraction.

nodes.label: SPEC_PATH prompt attribution of cache entries (#1939)
nodes.rationale: SPEC_PATH is the absolute path of references/extraction-spec.md shipped beside SKILL.md — the extraction prompt itself — and cache entries are attributed to it. When a graphify upgrade changes the prompt, entries produced by the old one are re-extracted rather than replayed, and unchanged prompts keep their entries (#1939). The SAME SPEC_PATH must be passed to both B0's read and B3's write, or the write lands where the next run will not look.

nodes.label: Only content files go to semantic extraction (#1392)
nodes.rationale: The semantic candidate list is built from only the 'document', 'paper' and 'image' categories. Code is already covered structurally by the AST pass, so flattening every category here would make subagents re-read every source file (#1392); video is not in the list because Step 2.5 has already turned it into a document.

nodes.label: Step B1 — split into chunks of 20-25 files
nodes.rationale: B1 loads .graphify_uncached.txt and splits it into chunks of 20-25 files each, giving every image its own chunk because vision needs separate context, and grouping files from the same directory together so related artifacts land in one chunk and cross-file relationships are more likely to be extracted.

nodes.label: Step B2 — dispatch ALL subagents in one message
nodes.rationale: One Agent tool call per chunk, all issued IN THE SAME RESPONSE — that is the only way they run in parallel; making one call, waiting, then making another is sequential and defeats the purpose. Each subagent gets the spec prompt with FILE_LIST, CHUNK_NUM, TOTAL_CHUNKS, DEEP_MODE and CHUNK_PATH substituted, where CHUNK_PATH is an absolute path derived from the cwd project root, not from .graphify_root (#1392).

nodes.label: subagent_type must be general-purpose, never Explore
nodes.rationale: Always use subagent_type="general-purpose". Explore is read-only and cannot write chunk files to disk, which silently drops extraction results; general-purpose has the Write and Bash access the subagent needs.

nodes.label: references/extraction-spec.md subagent prompt
nodes.rationale: The exact subagent prompt — JSON schema, node-ID rules, confidence rubric, frontmatter, hyperedge and vision rules — lives in references/extraction-spec.md and is passed verbatim. It is loaded only at Step B2 and only when at least one chunk holds a doc, paper or image; a pure-code corpus has skipped Part B and never reads it.

nodes.label: Step B3 — collect, cache and merge chunks
nodes.rationale: B3 waits for all subagents, concatenates every graphify-out/.graphify_chunk_*.json into .graphify_semantic_new.json (summing input/output tokens), saves the new results to cache, then merges cached + new into .graphify_semantic.json and removes the temporary .graphify_cached.json, .graphify_uncached.txt and .graphify_semantic_new.json.

nodes.label: Chunk file on disk is the success signal
nodes.rationale: Success is judged by whether graphify-out/.graphify_chunk_NN.json exists on disk and holds valid JSON with nodes and edges. A missing file means the subagent was likely dispatched read-only, and must produce the explicit warning 'chunk N missing from disk — subagent may have been read-only. Re-run with general-purpose agent.' — it is never silently skipped; an invalid-JSON chunk is warned about and skipped without aborting.

nodes.label: Stop if more than half the chunks failed
nodes.rationale: If more than half the chunks failed or are missing, the run stops and tells the user to re-run ensuring subagent_type="general-purpose" is used — a bulk failure is treated as a dispatch misconfiguration rather than partial data to proceed with.

nodes.label: graphify.cache.save_semantic_cache
nodes.rationale: save_semantic_cache(nodes, edges, hyperedges, root=INPUT_PATH, allowed_source_files=uncached, prompt_file=SPEC_PATH) persists the newly extracted fragments, restricted to the files actually dispatched this run, and returns the number of files cached.

nodes.label: Write real token counts back into each chunk
nodes.rationale: The chunk JSON a subagent writes always carries placeholder zero token counts. After each Agent call completes, the real counts must be read from the Agent tool result's `usage` field and written back into the chunk JSON before merging, otherwise the cost tracker and report understate the run.

nodes.label: Node deduplication by id
nodes.rationale: Both merges deduplicate nodes on their 'id' while keeping edges and hyperedges as a plain concatenation: B3 dedupes cached + new semantic nodes, and Part C seeds the seen-set from the AST nodes so AST wins and only unseen semantic nodes are appended.

nodes.label: Part C — merge AST + semantic into .graphify_extract.json
nodes.rationale: Part C reads .graphify_ast.json and .graphify_semantic.json, puts AST nodes first and appends semantic nodes not already seen by id, concatenates edges, carries hyperedges from the semantic side only, and writes graphify-out/.graphify_extract.json with the semantic token totals — printing 'Merged: N nodes, M edges (A AST + S semantic)'.

nodes.label: Step 4 — build, cluster, analyze, generate outputs
nodes.rationale: Step 4 loads the merged extraction and the detection JSON, builds the graph, checks the empty-graph guard, clusters, scores cohesion, computes god nodes / surprising connections / placeholder-labelled suggested questions, exports graph.json first, then writes GRAPH_REPORT.md and the .graphify_analysis.json sidecar, printing 'Graph: N nodes, M edges, C communities'.

nodes.label: graphify.build.build_from_json
nodes.rationale: build_from_json(extraction, root=INPUT_PATH, directed=IS_DIRECTED) returns the NetworkX graph G. The root= argument mirrors the --update runbook (#1361): it relativizes source_file to the same base so a full build and an incremental --update never drift apart on re-extract, and Step 5 must pass the identical root for node-key parity.

nodes.label: --directed builds a DiGraph
nodes.rationale: IS_DIRECTED must be substituted as True when --directed was given (building a DiGraph that preserves edge direction source→target) and otherwise False (the default undirected Graph). The literal placeholder must never be left in the code, and the same value is passed to Step 4.5's diagnostics and Step 5's rebuild.

nodes.label: Empty-graph stop before any write
nodes.rationale: Immediately after build and BEFORE any write, if G.number_of_nodes() == 0 the run prints 'ERROR: Graph is empty - extraction produced no nodes.' plus the possible causes (all files skipped, binary-only corpus, or extraction failed) and raises SystemExit(1), so an empty extraction can never clobber a good graph.json, GRAPH_REPORT.md or analysis sidecar (#1392). The agent must stop there and not proceed to labeling or visualization.

nodes.label: graphify.cluster.cluster
nodes.rationale: cluster(G) returns the community structure as a mapping of community id to members; it is the expensive step that --no-cluster skips and the only step --cluster-only reruns against an existing graph.

nodes.label: graphify.cluster.score_all (cohesion)
nodes.rationale: score_all(G, communities) returns a per-community cohesion score, carried into generate() and persisted in .graphify_analysis.json under 'cohesion'. The Honesty Rules require the raw number to be shown rather than hidden behind symbols.

nodes.label: graphify.analyze — god_nodes, surprising_connections, suggest_questions
nodes.rationale: god_nodes(G) surfaces the highest-connectivity hub nodes, surprising_connections(G, communities) surfaces cross-community bridges, and suggest_questions(G, communities, labels) proposes questions the graph can answer. Step 4 runs suggest_questions with placeholder 'Community N' labels and Step 5 regenerates it with the curated labels, because labels affect question phrasing.

nodes.label: graphify.report.generate
nodes.rationale: generate(G, communities, cohesion, labels, gods, surprises, detection, tokens, INPUT_PATH, suggested_questions=questions) returns the markdown audit report written to graphify-out/GRAPH_REPORT.md. The tokens argument carries {'input','output'} taken from the extraction, which is how the Honesty Rule 'always show token cost in the report' is satisfied.

nodes.label: graphify.export.to_json
nodes.rationale: to_json(G, communities, 'graphify-out/graph.json') writes the graph and returns a boolean: False means it wrote nothing. Step 5 calls it again with community_labels=labels so graph.json nodes carry the curated community_name (#2490).

nodes.label: #479 shrink guard
nodes.rationale: to_json honours the #479 shrink guard: it returns False and writes nothing when the new graph is smaller than the existing graph.json. The runbook then prints 'ERROR: refused to shrink graphify-out/graph.json (existing graph has more nodes; #479).' and advises re-running a full build with --force if the shrink is intentional. In Step 5 the same extraction is used, so the guard should pass on node count; if it still refuses, surface the message and do not force past it.

nodes.label: Export FIRST, then report and sidecar (#1392)
nodes.rationale: graph.json is exported before GRAPH_REPORT.md and the analysis sidecar are written, and those two are written only when to_json actually wrote — so the report can never describe a graph that graph.json does not contain (#1392).

nodes.label: .graphify_analysis.json sidecar
nodes.rationale: Step 4 writes graphify-out/.graphify_analysis.json holding communities, cohesion (both string-keyed), gods, surprises and questions. Step 5 reads it back, coercing the community and cohesion keys to int, so the labeling pass does not need to recluster.

nodes.label: Step 4.5 — graph health check (read-only integrity gate)
nodes.rationale: A non-destructive diagnostic on the extraction, run before labeling. It surfaces edge collapse, dangling/missing endpoints and self-loops — the silent-corruption modes of incremental updates and AST/LLM id mismatches. It is read-only and never aborts; a GRAPH HEALTH WARNING must be surfaced in the final summary per the Honesty Rules, but the graph stays usable.

nodes.label: graphify.diagnostics — diagnose_extraction / format_diagnostic_report
nodes.rationale: diagnose_extraction(extraction, directed=IS_DIRECTED, root=INPUT_PATH) returns a summary dict with the counter keys dangling_endpoint_edges, missing_endpoint_edges, self_loop_edges, directed_same_endpoint_collapsed_edges and undirected_same_endpoint_collapsed_edges; format_diagnostic_report(summary) renders it. Any non-zero counter turns the printed line into 'GRAPH HEALTH WARNING: ... - graph may be incomplete/corrupt.', otherwise 'Graph health: OK'.

nodes.label: Step 5 — label communities
nodes.rationale: The agent reads .graphify_analysis.json and, for each community key, writes a 2-5 word plain-language name from its node labels (e.g. 'Attention Mechanism', 'Training Pipeline', 'Data Loading'). It then rebuilds G with the same root and directed flag, regenerates the suggested questions with the real labels, rewrites GRAPH_REPORT.md, and saves the names to graphify-out/.graphify_labels.json for the visualizer.

nodes.label: Re-export so graph.json carries community_name (#2490)
nodes.rationale: After labeling, Step 5 calls to_json(..., community_labels=labels) a second time so graph.json nodes carry the curated community_name (#2490). Because the extraction is the same as Step 4's, the #479 shrink guard is expected to pass on node count.

nodes.label: Step 6 — HTML always, Obsidian vault opt-in
nodes.rationale: `graphify export html` runs on every run unless --no-viz. `graphify export obsidian` runs only when --obsidian was explicitly given — it generates one file per node — and honours --obsidian-dir by passing --dir, otherwise defaulting to graphify-out/obsidian.

nodes.label: 5,000-node HTML aggregation and warning
nodes.rationale: `graphify export html` auto-aggregates to a community view when the graph exceeds 5,000 nodes, and the Honesty Rules forbid running HTML visualization on a graph with more than 5,000 nodes without warning the user.

nodes.label: Steps 6b-8 — flag-gated exports and benchmark
nodes.rationale: Wiki, Neo4j, FalkorDB, SVG, GraphML and MCP run only when their flag is present (--wiki, --neo4j/--neo4j-push, --falkordb/--falkordb-push, --svg, --graphml, --mcp), and the token-reduction benchmark runs when total_words exceeds 5,000. A default run with no export flags skips all of them, and any --wiki export must run before Step 9 cleanup so .graphify_labels.json is still available.

nodes.label: Step 9 — save manifest, cost tracker, cleanup, report
nodes.rationale: The final step saves the manifest that --update reads, appends this run to the cumulative cost tracker, deletes the temp files, and prints the completion block naming graph.html, GRAPH_REPORT.md, graph.json and (only if --obsidian) obsidian/, plus the sponsor link.

nodes.label: graphify.detect.save_manifest
nodes.rationale: save_manifest(manifest_files, root=INPUT_PATH, scan_corpus=..., clear_semantic=...) writes the on-disk manifest that a later --update matches against. root= relativizes the manifest keys to the scan root — the same base as the build — so the manifest is portable across clones and machines and --update matches cached files instead of missing every one (#1417).

nodes.label: _stamped_manifest_files — stamp only what produced output (#2015)
nodes.rationale: graphify.cli._stamped_manifest_files(corpus, extract, Path(INPUT_PATH)) stamps only the semantic files (docs/papers/images) that ACTUALLY produced output: a detected file whose chunk failed or was omitted must stay unstamped so the next --update re-queues it, otherwise it is marked done and its content is lost forever (#2015). Code files are always stamped because AST is deterministic.

nodes.label: clear_semantic — drop stale semantic hashes (#1948)
nodes.rationale: Files dispatched this run but not stamped still carry a stale semantic_hash from a prior run, so the difference (dispatched minus stamped) is passed as clear_semantic; without it detect_incremental would read them as unchanged and never re-queue them (#1948).

nodes.label: scan_corpus = the RAW full corpus (#1908)
nodes.rationale: scan_corpus is the raw full corpus (detect['all_files'] or detect['files']), not the stamp-filtered subset, so in-root files newly excluded since the last run are dropped rather than masquerading as deletions, while untouched files' prior rows are still preserved (#1908).

nodes.label: graphify-out/cost.json cumulative cost tracker
nodes.rationale: Step 9 appends {date, input_tokens, output_tokens, files} to cost.json's 'runs' list and adds to total_input_tokens/total_output_tokens, creating the file if absent, then prints both this run's and the all-time totals with the run count.

nodes.label: Temp-file cleanup at Step 9
nodes.rationale: The run ends by removing .graphify_detect.json, .graphify_extract.json, .graphify_ast.json, .graphify_semantic.json and .graphify_analysis.json, deleting every .graphify_chunk_*.json at depth 1, and clearing .needs_update.

nodes.label: Paste only God Nodes, Surprising Connections, Suggested Questions
nodes.rationale: After the completion block, exactly three sections of GRAPH_REPORT.md are pasted into the chat — God Nodes, Surprising Connections and Suggested Questions. The full report is explicitly not pasted; the output must stay concise.

nodes.label: Offer to trace the most interesting question
nodes.rationale: The agent picks the single suggested question that crosses the most community boundaries or has the most surprising bridge node and offers to trace it; on yes it runs /graphify query on that question and walks the user through the path, ending each answer with a natural follow-up so the session feels like navigation. 'The graph is the map. Your job after the pipeline is to be the guide.'

nodes.label: Interpreter guard for subcommands
nodes.rationale: Before running --update, --cluster-only, query, path, explain or add, the agent checks that graphify-out/.graphify_python exists; if the user deleted graphify-out/ it re-resolves the interpreter from the graphify binary's shebang (rejecting shell-unsafe characters and falling back to python3) and rewrites the marker file.

nodes.label: --update and --cluster-only subcommands
nodes.rationale: Both are non-default subcommands: --update re-extracts only new or changed files (driven by the manifest), and --cluster-only reruns clustering on the existing graph. Their flows live in references/update.md.

nodes.label: /graphify query — answer from the graph
nodes.rationale: When graphify-out/graph.json already exists and the user asks about the corpus, the agent answers from the graph rather than rebuilding it: `graphify query "<question>"`, BFS by default for broad context, --dfs to trace a specific path, --budget N to cap the answer. It must answer using only what the graph output contains and quote source_location when citing a specific fact.

nodes.label: Vocabulary expansion before traversal
nodes.rationale: Before traversal the question is expanded against the graph's own vocabulary so a wording mismatch does not collapse the answer to noise. The mechanics live in references/query.md alongside the BFS/DFS modes, the --budget cap and save-result feedback.

nodes.label: Inline NetworkX traversal fallback
nodes.rationale: If the `graphify query` CLI is unavailable, the agent falls back to an inline NetworkX traversal of graphify-out/graph.json rather than rebuilding the graph or refusing the question.

nodes.label: /graphify path and /graphify explain
nodes.rationale: `graphify path "A" "B"` returns the shortest path between two concepts and `graphify explain "X"` returns a plain-language explanation of a node; both flows are documented in references/query.md.

nodes.label: /graphify add and --watch
nodes.rationale: Neither is part of the default build. `graphify add <url>` fetches a URL into ./raw and updates the graph, optionally tagging --author (who wrote it) and --contributor (who added it to the corpus); --watch watches a folder and auto-rebuilds on code changes with no LLM needed. Both flows live in references/add-watch.md.

nodes.label: Commit hook and native CLAUDE.md integration
nodes.rationale: Installing the post-commit auto-rebuild hook or wiring graphify into a project's CLAUDE.md is out of the main pipeline and documented in references/hooks.md.

nodes.label: Honesty Rules
nodes.rationale: Five closing rules: never invent an edge (use AMBIGUOUS if unsure); never skip the corpus check warning; always show token cost in the report; never hide cohesion scores behind symbols — show the raw number; never run HTML viz on a graph with more than 5,000 nodes without warning the user.

nodes.label: EXTRACTED / INFERRED / AMBIGUOUS audit trail
nodes.rationale: Every edge carries an honest confidence tier — EXTRACTED, INFERRED or AMBIGUOUS — which is what makes the graph auditable and persistent across sessions; the confidence rubric itself lives in references/extraction-spec.md.

nodes.label: graphify-out/graph.json
nodes.rationale: graph.json is the raw GraphRAG-ready graph data and the file whose existence triggers the query fast path. It is the artifact both write-guards protect, and Step 5 rewrites it so its nodes carry community_name.

nodes.label: graphify-out/GRAPH_REPORT.md
nodes.rationale: GRAPH_REPORT.md is the plain-language audit report holding cohesion scores, token cost, God Nodes, Surprising Connections and Suggested Questions. It is written twice — once with placeholder community labels in Step 4 and again with curated labels in Step 5.

nodes.label: httpx corpus evaluation (2026-04-03)
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: A worked evaluation dated 2026-04-03 of what graphify actually produced on a 6-file synthetic httpx-like Python corpus, scored across six dimensions and ending at an overall 5.7/10. The evaluator was Claude Sonnet 4.6.

nodes.label: 6-file synthetic httpx corpus
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: The corpus under test is a synthetic httpx-like Python codebase of 6 files (exceptions, models, auth, utils, client, transport) totalling roughly 2,800 words. graphify's own corpus check verdict was that it is large enough that graph structure adds value.

nodes.label: Analytical simulation, not a live run
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: Bash execution was unavailable, so the review is a full deterministic code trace of every graphify source module against the corpus rather than an executed build. Node/edge counts and community assignments are ESTIMATED from code logic, and the exact Leiden partition is non-deterministic; only the structural analysis is claimed sound.

nodes.label: graphify AST-only pipeline
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: The pipeline exercised is graphify's AST extractor plus graph_builder, Leiden clusterer, analyzer and reporter. For code corpora it relies entirely on tree-sitter; the LLM-driven richer extraction pass the skill doc envisions applies to document/paper corpora, not this path.

nodes.label: Observed graph: ~95 nodes, ~130 edges, 4 communities
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: The reported GRAPH_REPORT.md for this corpus shows roughly 95 nodes, 130 edges and 4 detected communities, with an extraction mix of ~100% EXTRACTED, 0% INFERRED, 0% AMBIGUOUS.

nodes.label: Zero token cost
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: The run's reported token cost is 0 input and 0 output — the AST path spends no LLM tokens at all.

nodes.label: 100% EXTRACTED, 0% INFERRED
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: Every edge in the observed graph is EXTRACTED because all of them come from the tree-sitter parse; there are zero INFERRED and zero AMBIGUOUS edges. The review calls this honest but not semantically rich, and scores edge accuracy 5/10 on that basis.

nodes.label: God-node ranking observed
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: The top-10 god nodes are client.py (~28 edges), models.py (~22), transport.py (~20), exceptions.py (~18), BaseClient (~15), auth.py (~14), Response (~12), Client (~10), AsyncClient (~10), utils.py (~9). Scored 7/10: the core abstractions are identified, but file nodes dominate the top spots.

nodes.label: Synthetic file hub nodes inflate degree
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: The extractor creates one synthetic node per file and a `contains` edge from it to every class and function in that file, so a 300-line file with 20 definitions gets 20 edges from one artificial hub. These are not real code entities, yet they outrank genuine abstractions like BaseClient (15 connections).

nodes.label: Fix: exclude file nodes from god-node ranking
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: Proposed remedy for the file-hub distortion in analyzer.py god_nodes(): exclude nodes whose label ends in `.py`, or subtract file-contains edges from the degree count, and report file nodes separately as "Module Hubs".

nodes.label: 14 inheritance edges silently dropped
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: Issue 1, rated CRITICAL: all 14 inheritance edges in exceptions.py are dropped without an error, so chains like RequestError -> TransportError -> TimeoutException -> ConnectTimeout are invisible and the hierarchy appears flat.

nodes.label: External base class never registered as a node
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: The root cause of the dropped inheritance edges: ast_extractor.py builds an inheritance target as `_make_id(stem, base_name)`, so `RequestError(Exception)` yields target `exceptions_exception`. Because `Exception` (and ABC, dict, Mapping) is never registered in `seen_ids`, that target does not exist.

nodes.label: Edge clean step drops unresolvable endpoints
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: The cleanup at ast_extractor.py lines 143-149 checks that endpoints are in valid_ids and silently discards any edge that is not an import relation. Import edges to external modules (typing, hashlib, json, re, time, socket) are exempted and kept, which the review judges correct behaviour.

nodes.label: Within-file inheritance is captured
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: When the parent class is defined in the same file the stem matches and the edge survives: `Client(BaseClient)` and `AsyncClient(BaseClient)` both resolve to `client_baseclient`, and `HTTPTransport(BaseTransport)` resolves to `transport_basetransport`. The review calls this a good sign — the failure is specific to bases that are never defined in the corpus.

nodes.label: Fix: stub nodes for external base classes
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: Proposed remedy: create stub nodes for external base classes labelled "(external)" rather than dropping the edge, or keep inheritance edges regardless of whether the target node exists.

nodes.label: Exception community held together only by the file node
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: Community 2 groups all 15 exception classes, but because every inheritance edge was dropped the only intra-community edges are `exceptions.py contains ExceptionClass`. Cohesion is near-zero (0.10 estimated) and the members look like isolated nodes hanging off a file hub, which may make Leiden cluster them poorly.

nodes.label: Transport and Auth merged into one community
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: Issue 3 (MODERATE): Community 3 bundles HTTPTransport, ConnectionPool, ProxyTransport with BasicAuth, DigestAuth, BearerAuth and NetRCAuth purely because both modules import from models.py and exceptions.py. They are architecturally distinct layers a developer would want split into "Transport Layer" and "Auth Handlers".

nodes.label: Sparse connectivity defeats Leiden layer separation
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: auth.py and transport.py have no direct structural link to each other, so with too few edges Leiden groups them anyway. The review attributes this to sparse connectivity in a codebase whose layered architecture never manifests as structural links inside each file.

nodes.label: Fix: edge file-type metadata or module-first clustering
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: Proposed remedy for clusterer.py: add file-type metadata to edges so the clusterer can penalise cross-layer grouping, or cluster at module level first (treating files as nodes) before drilling down to class and method level.

nodes.label: Cohesion 0.08-0.18, honest and uninflated
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: Observed community cohesion ranges from 0.08 (Transport & Auth) through 0.10 (Exceptions) and 0.14 (Core HTTP Client) to 0.18 (Request/Response Models). The review reads the low values as correctly reflecting a real codebase with cross-cutting concerns rather than as artificially inflated scores.

nodes.label: Surprising connections are mostly obvious imports
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: Scored 4/10. All five reported connections are EXTRACTED cross-file import edges, and 3 of 5 (transport->exceptions, client->auth, transport->models) are mundane imports; ProxyTransport<->TransportError is called an outright false positive since transport.py imports exceptions directly.

nodes.label: DigestAuth <-> Response: the one real insight
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: The genuinely non-obvious surfaced connection: DigestAuth must inspect the Response (WWW-Authenticate header, 401 status) to build its challenge, so auth is a request-response cycle participant rather than a pure pre-request decorator. The graph surfaces it but does not explain it — it is buried as EXTRACTED connection #4.

nodes.label: Confidence sort degenerates when all edges are EXTRACTED
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: analyzer.py _cross_file_surprises() sorts AMBIGUOUS -> INFERRED -> EXTRACTED to surface uncertain connections first, but on an all-EXTRACTED graph the key is constant and the ordering falls back to arbitrary. The ranking mechanism provides no differentiation on AST-only corpora.

nodes.label: Fix: rank surprises by import distance
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: Proposed remedy: add a distance metric preferring pairs whose source files have no direct import relationship, so `transport.py -> exceptions.py` ranks below `DigestAuth -> Response` because transport already imports exceptions.

nodes.label: Import edges do not name what is imported
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: `client.py imports_from models` is correct but low-signal: it does not record WHICH names, so the graph cannot distinguish that Client specifically uses Request and Response rather than the whole models module.

nodes.label: No call edges at all
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: The AST extractor emits no "calls", "conceptually_related_to" or "implements" relations. `Response.raise_for_status()` calling `HTTPStatusError()` and `DigestAuth.auth_flow` reading `Response.status_code` are both architecturally critical and entirely invisible.

nodes.label: Fix: lightweight name-based call-detection pass
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: Proposed remedy for issue 4: scan function bodies for name references to add a lightweight call-detection pass. Even simple name-based heuristics would contribute INFERRED edges for common patterns without an LLM.

nodes.label: _make_id method-edge fix confirmed working
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: Issue 6, verified: a method node ID is `_make_id(parent_class_nid, func_name)` and the method edge `add_edge(parent_class_nid, func_nid, "method", line)` uses the same parent id, so both endpoints are in seen_ids and method edges survive cleanup. On ~45 methods this preserves roughly 35-40 edges that would otherwise be dropped.

nodes.label: Previously reported 27% edge drop
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: An earlier bug in which method edges were built with IDs different from the registered method node IDs, causing a reported 27% edge drop. The review finds it fixed in this version — no 27% drop for method edges.

nodes.label: Concept-node filtering confirmed working
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: Issue 7, verified: analyzer.py `_is_concept_node()` filters nodes with an empty source_file or a source_file with no extension. The AST extractor always sets source_file to a real path, so no concept nodes leak in and the surprising-connections section shows only real code entities.

nodes.label: AST-only extraction has a semantic ceiling
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: Structural extraction alone is judged to capture at most 25-30% of the interesting relationships in a Python codebase (elsewhere stated as ~20% of the semantically interesting ones). The extractor is deterministic, fast and accurate for what it captures, but produces a structurally correct, semantically thin graph — the skeleton without the architectural intent.

nodes.label: Corpus is small for graph analysis
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: At ~2,800 words and 6 files this corpus is on the small side; the skill doc's own warning that a corpus fitting in one context window may not need a graph applies. Real httpx has 30+ files, and graph value would rise substantially where file-level connectivity creates meaningful community structure.

nodes.label: ~85% of meaningful code entities captured
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: Node/edge quality scores 6/10: file nodes for all 6 files, every top-level class, module-level functions from utils.py and auth.py, and methods on all classes are captured — about 85% of meaningful entities. The main gaps are the exception inheritance chain and cross-file import references to specific names.

nodes.label: Property decorator context lost
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: Properties such as url, content, cookies, is_success and is_error are extracted as ordinary methods, with no semantic distinction preserving that they were decorated as properties.

nodes.label: Overall score 5.7/10 across six dimensions
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: The six dimension scores are node/edge quality 6, edge accuracy 5, community quality 6, surprising connections 4, god nodes 7, overall usefulness 6 — averaging 5.7/10. Estimated edge breakdown: ~115 correct (88%), ~14 silently dropped (11%), ~2 false positives.

nodes.label: What a 9/10 graph would look like
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: The stated target state: inheritance edges preserved via stub external base classes, call-graph edges added even heuristically (raise_for_status -> HTTPStatusError), Transport and Auth in distinct communities, surprising connections filtered to real cross-cutting surprises, file hub nodes excluded from god-node ranking, and at least some INFERRED edges for shared data structures and naming patterns.

nodes.label: Karpathy repos + papers benchmark corpus
nodes.rationale: The benchmark corpus is a MULTI-SOURCE mix: nanoGPT, minGPT and micrograd (3 repos) plus 5 attention/transformer research papers and 4 images — 29 Python files, 14 docs/READMEs, 5 PDFs and 4 images, 52 files total, ~92,616 words and ~123,488 naive full-context tokens, measured 2026-04-04.

nodes.label: Hybrid extraction: AST for code, LLM for prose
nodes.rationale: The run used two extraction paths over one corpus: AST (tree-sitter, deterministic) for the 29 code files and Claude semantic extraction for docs, papers and images. The resulting graph carries both tiers side by side (163 AST + 112 semantic nodes).

nodes.label: AST (tree-sitter) code extraction arm
nodes.rationale: Deterministic tree-sitter parsing of the 29 Python files, with no LLM involved. It contributed 163 of the 285 nodes and 281 of the 340 edges, and is also the arm that emits raw import edges to stdlib names.

nodes.label: Claude semantic extraction of docs, papers and images
nodes.rationale: Claude semantic extraction over the 14 docs/READMEs, 5 PDFs and 4 images produced 112 semantic nodes and 97 semantic edges, and is credited with finding the FlashAttention-to-CausalSelfAttention bridge that the AST arm could not see.

nodes.label: Code-only reduction ratio 8.8x
nodes.rationale: Over the 29 code files alone (~16,997 corpus tokens, no Claude involved), the average BFS-subgraph query cost was ~1,929 tokens, an 8.8x reduction against naive full-context stuffing.

nodes.label: Full-corpus reduction ratio 71.5x
nodes.rationale: Over all 52 files (~123,488 naive tokens) the average BFS-subgraph query cost was ~1,726 tokens — a 71.5x reduction. The headline figure is corpus-conditional: it belongs to this 92k-word mixed corpus, not to the tool in general.

nodes.label: BFS subgraph cost stays roughly constant
nodes.rationale: The observed mechanism behind the reduction: the returned BFS subgraph stays roughly constant at ~1,700 tokens regardless of corpus size, while naive context stuffing scales linearly with the corpus.

nodes.label: Reduction ratio grows with corpus size
nodes.rationale: Because subgraph cost is flat and naive stuffing is linear, the ratio is a function of corpus size: 8.8x on the 17k-token code subset, 71.5x on the 123k-token full corpus, and a projected ~2k vs 670k tokens on a 500k-word research library.

nodes.label: Per-question reduction varies 43.5x to 126.7x
nodes.rationale: The 71.5x average hides a wide per-question spread over the same graph: 126.7x for 'what connects micrograd to nanoGPT', 100.8x for the FlashAttention memory question, 68.6x for core abstractions and error handling, and 43.5x for the attention-mechanism question.

nodes.label: Cross-source hub question returns a bigger subgraph
nodes.rationale: The 'how does the attention mechanism work' query returned 2,836 tokens — the largest subgraph and the weakest 43.5x ratio — precisely because four sources converge on it: FlashAttention, nanoGPT CausalSelfAttention, minGPT CausalSelfAttention and the AttnRes paper.

nodes.label: CausalSelfAttention nodes in both GPT repos
nodes.rationale: CausalSelfAttention exists as an AST node in both nanoGPT and minGPT. Duplicated across repos, it becomes the convergence point that the FlashAttention paper cluster bridges into and that inflates the attention query's subgraph.

nodes.label: Merged graph: 285 nodes, 340 edges, 53 communities
nodes.rationale: The merged multi-source graph held 285 nodes (163 AST + 112 semantic), 340 edges (281 AST + 97 semantic, counted AFTER pruning) and 53 communities. The AST tier outnumbers the semantic tier on both nodes and, far more sharply, edges.

nodes.label: 53 communities = 17 major + 36 isolates
nodes.rationale: Of 53 detected communities only 17 are major (30 down to 5 nodes: nanoGPT model architecture, minGPT training, nanoGPT training pipeline, micrograd NN layer, FlashAttention paper, BPE tokenizer, micrograd autograd engine, and so on); the remaining 36 are single-node isolates.

nodes.label: Leiden community detection over the merged graph
nodes.rationale: Leiden is the clustering algorithm that produced the 53 communities. The review credits it by name with finding real architectural boundaries — the nanoGPT model/training split — and with co-clustering files from different repos that never import each other.

nodes.label: God nodes by degree in the merged graph
nodes.rationale: The four highest-degree nodes were micrograd `Value` (15 edges), nanoGPT `Training Script` (11), nanoGPT `GPT` (9) and micrograd `Layer` (8). Notably all four are CODE nodes — no paper or image node reached the top of the degree ranking.

nodes.label: micrograd Value as the top god node
nodes.rationale: `Value` in micrograd's engine took the highest degree at 15 edges because it is the autograd primitive: everything math-related in the smallest repo connects through it, so the tiniest source produced the graph's most central node.

nodes.label: micrograd split into engine and nn communities
nodes.rationale: Clustering split micrograd into two separate communities — the autograd engine (`Value`, `backward`, `__add__`, `__mul__`) and the nn layer (`Layer`, `__call__`, `MLP`) — matching the architecture split the repo itself intends.

nodes.label: nanoGPT model definition separated from training loop
nodes.rationale: Communities 0 and 2 correctly separate nanoGPT's model definition from its training loop — different concerns living in different files, and the review states Leiden found that boundary without being told about it.

nodes.label: BPETokenizer correctly clustered standalone
nodes.rationale: `bpe.py` formed its own 17-node cluster (`BPETokenizer`, `decode`, `bytes_to_unicode`, the full tokenisation logic) rather than being absorbed into the model or trainer community — a correct standalone identification, not an isolate defect.

nodes.label: Cross-repo INFERRED edge between the two Block classes
nodes.rationale: The graph linked nanoGPT `Block` to minGPT `Block` on structural similarity — same class name, similar methods — producing a cross-repo INFERRED edge. The review judges it genuine: both implement the same GPT block pattern.

nodes.label: FlashAttention paper community (Community 5)
nodes.rationale: A 21-node semantic community covering IO-awareness, HBM/SRAM, recomputation and BERT/GPT-2 benchmarks, extracted from the FlashAttention PDF — the largest paper cluster in the corpus.

nodes.label: Paper-to-code cross-community bridge
nodes.rationale: The FlashAttention cluster bridging into CausalSelfAttention in both nanoGPT and minGPT forms the ONLY paper-to-code cross-community edges in the whole graph — cross-tier connection happened, but exactly once.

nodes.label: Images extracted into semantic nodes
nodes.rationale: The four images were read correctly: `gpt2_124M_loss.png` yielded 'val_loss=2.905 at step 399', `gout.svg` was recognised as micrograd's computation graph, and `moon_mlp.png` as an MLP decision boundary.

nodes.label: 94 stdlib import validation warnings
nodes.rationale: Imports of `setuptools`, `os`, `math` and `sys` produced 94 'target does not match any node' validation warnings, because the AST extractor emits import edges to stdlib names before the validator can prune them; the edges are discarded but inflate the pre-pruning edge count.

nodes.label: Edge pruning of unresolvable targets
nodes.rationale: A validation pass discards edges whose target matches no node, which is why the reported 340 edges are explicitly stated as an after-pruning figure and why the stdlib import edges never reach the final graph.

nodes.label: Config-only files become single-node communities
nodes.rationale: Config scripts with no functions — `eval_gpt2.py`, `eval_gpt2_large.py` and similar — have nothing to connect to, so each lands as its own single-node community. Expected behaviour, but it adds roughly 36 trivial communities.

nodes.label: Isolate noise: 36 of 53 communities are single nodes
nodes.rationale: The review calls this 'the main cost is honesty': 53 communities where 17 are real and 36 are isolates. Not merging isolates is correct behaviour, but the reported community count and the visualisation both become misleadingly noisy — the code-only run's 17-community figure read cleaner.

nodes.label: Proposed --min-community-size flag
nodes.rationale: The review's suggested remedy for isolate noise is a future `--min-community-size` flag that filters trivial communities out of the presentation without merging isolates into clusters they do not belong to.

nodes.label: Papers not deep-linked to implementation
nodes.rationale: The FlashAttention cluster knows the '3x GPT-2 speedup' claim but the graph never links that claim to the specific `CausalSelfAttention` implementation that would benefit — the observed weak spot is claim-level paper-to-implementation linking, not paper-to-concept linking.

nodes.label: --mode deep extraction pass
nodes.rationale: The named remedy for shallow paper-to-implementation links is running the paper extraction pass with `--mode deep` and explicit cross-file context; this benchmark did not use it.

nodes.label: Value.backward() to Trainer.run() cross-repo link
nodes.rationale: The graph surfaced `micrograd/engine.py::Value.backward()` connecting to `minGPT/mingpt/trainer.py::Trainer.run()` unprompted — both implement the same forward/backward pattern at very different scales, across repos.

nodes.label: Co-clustering through shared vocabulary, not imports
nodes.rationale: `nanoGPT/train.py` and `minGPT/mingpt/trainer.py` landed in the same community despite being in different repos and never importing each other; Leiden found the structural similarity through shared vocabulary — optimizer, scheduler, gradient clipping.

nodes.label: Cross-repo linkage without any import path
nodes.rationale: The corpus condition that makes this benchmark instructive for merged multi-source graphs: three repos with no dependency on each other still got connected — by name/structure similarity, by shared vocabulary co-clustering, and by a paper cluster bridging into both GPT repos.

nodes.label: Verdict: strong on structure and concepts, weak on claim-to-code
nodes.rationale: The closing verdict grades the graph as high for code structure, strong for paper-to-concept connections (semantic extraction found the FlashAttention-to-CausalSelfAttention bridge), and weaker on direct paper-to-implementation links — with 71.5x reduction as the headline number.

nodes.label: Mixed-corpus graphify evaluation (2026-04-04)
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: A live end-to-end evaluation of graphify over a MIXED corpus of 5 files — 3 Python files (analyze.py, build.py, cluster.py), 1 markdown paper (attention_notes.md) and 1 Arabic PNG image (attention_arabic.png), ~4,020 words in total. It scored 9.0/10 overall and is explicitly framed as a strong pass 'with a small corpus'.

nodes.label: detect → extract → build → cluster → analyze → query → feedback pipeline
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: The evaluated pipeline is stated verbatim as: detect → extract (AST) → build → cluster → analyze → query → feedback loop. Each stage was exercised live against the real graph.json rather than simulated.

nodes.label: Corpus detection by file class
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: detect() classified the 5-file corpus as code:3, paper:1, image:1 — all correct, scoring 10/10 on detection accuracy. Classification is per-file and drives which extraction path each file takes.

nodes.label: Paper-signal regex heuristic
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: attention_notes.md was classified as `paper` rather than `document` because it contains \arxiv\b, \bdoi\s*:, \babstract\b, a `[1]` citation pattern and \d{4}\.\d{5} (1706.03762). The evaluator concludes the paper signal heuristic works correctly.

nodes.label: Corpus-size / single-context-window warning
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: At ~4,020 words detection emitted 'fits in a single context window — you may not need a graph'. The evaluator calls this honest and correct: the graph adds value at scale, not on 5-file repos.

nodes.label: AST extraction over the three Python files
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: AST extraction yielded analyze.py 9 nodes/9 edges, build.py 3/3 and cluster.py 6/7 — 18 nodes and 19 edges total. It scored 7/10: function and file nodes are correct, but there are no cross-file edges.

nodes.label: External dependency nodes added at build
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: The built graph has 20 nodes against 18 extracted, because 2 external dependency nodes (networkx, graspologic) are added. Those synthetic nodes are the only structure joining otherwise independent modules.

nodes.label: Community detection over the mixed graph
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: Three communities were found — Graph Analysis (analyze.py), Clustering & Scoring (cluster.py) and Graph Building (build.py) — mapping cleanly onto the three functional modules. Community quality scored 9/10.

nodes.label: Per-community cohesion score
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: Measured cohesion: Graph Building 0.50, Clustering & Scoring 0.29, Graph Analysis 0.22. build.py scores highest because it is a tight, self-contained module; cohesion here tracks intra-community edge density.

nodes.label: analyze.py's standalone passes make its subgraph sparse
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: analyze.py has the lowest cohesion (0.22) because its functions do not call each other — each is a standalone analysis pass — so its subgraph is sparse. Low cohesion here reflects module style, not an extraction defect.

nodes.label: Zero surprising connections on cleanly-layered code
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: The analysis surfaced 0 surprising connections and this is filed as NOT a bug: the three modules import nothing from each other, so there are no cross-community edges to surprise with. Surprising connections require a less cleanly separated codebase.

nodes.label: Modules connected only through an external dep node
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: Query Q1 found that cluster.py and build.py are linked via the `graspologic_partition` external dependency node — the shared dep, not any direct call or import, is what makes the two modules reachable from each other.

nodes.label: Live BFS query traversal
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: Three queries ran live against the real graph.json, each BFS-ing from a seed symbol: Q1 from cluster() reached 20 nodes (the full graph, because the corpus is small), Q2 from analyze.py reached 12, Q3 from cluster()+cohesion_score() reached 18. Query traversal scored 8/10.

nodes.label: Source-location citation in query answers
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: Query Q2 cited the source location correctly as `analyze.py:L1`, which the evaluation counts toward the query-traversal score. Answers therefore carry a file:line anchor back to the code they came from.

nodes.label: Feedback loop: answers filed back into the corpus
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: PASS, 10/10: all 3 saved query answers appeared in the next detect() scan (3/3) and will be extracted as nodes on the next --update. The evaluator's summary is that 'the graph grows from what you ask, not just what you add.'

nodes.label: graphify-out/memory/ answer store
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: Each query answer was written as a markdown file under graphify-out/memory/ (3 files, 1,528–1,838 bytes, named query_..._<question-slug>.md). Those files are ordinary corpus documents, which is what makes them re-detectable.

nodes.label: Arabic image OCR via Claude vision
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: The Arabic PNG of Transformer notes was read natively by Claude vision — no preprocessing, no reshaper libraries, no bidi algorithms. The evaluator states the model reads Arabic, Persian, Hebrew and Chinese identically to English; scored 10/10.

nodes.label: An image node is just a path; the vision subagent does the rest
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: graphify stores an image only as a path node; all semantic content comes from the vision subagent that reads the file. That division is why no language-specific machinery lives in graphify itself.

nodes.label: Concepts extracted from the Arabic image
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: From the Arabic notes graphify would extract MultiHeadAttention (h=8, d_model=512, d_k=d_v=64), PositionalEncoding, LayerNorm and Transformer (6 encoder + 6 decoder layers), plus the citation Vaswani et al. 2017, arXiv:1706.03762.

nodes.label: Issue 1 — suggest_questions() returns empty
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: suggest_questions() needs a community_labels dict and enough signal (AMBIGUOUS edges, bridge nodes, underexplored god nodes); on this small corpus with none of those it returns an empty list. Behaviour is correct, but the skill should handle the empty case gracefully.

nodes.label: Issue 2 — god_nodes() empty when every entity is file-level
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: god_nodes() correctly excludes file hub nodes, but on a 3-file corpus whose only real entities are file-level functions that leaves an empty result and the evaluation fell back to manual degree ranking. Proposed fix: emit a 'corpus too small for meaningful god nodes' notice instead of a silent empty list.

nodes.label: AST-only extraction produces no INFERRED edges
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: The evaluation names edge-level semantics as a primary gap: an AST-only pass yields no INFERRED edges, so the code layer carries structural edges only. The paper and image material stayed semantically separate from the extracted code graph.

nodes.label: Six-dimension scorecard, 9.0/10 overall
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: Scores: detection accuracy 10/10, AST extraction 7/10, community quality 9/10, query traversal 8/10, feedback loop 10/10, Arabic OCR 10/10 — overall 9.0/10, with the remaining gaps being edge-level semantics and god_nodes/suggest_questions behaviour on tiny corpora.

nodes.label: Small-corpus condition on every finding
nodes.author: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.rationale: Every observation here is conditioned on a 5-file, ~4,020-word corpus: BFS reaching 'the full graph' is a corpus-size artifact, both minor issues are attributed to corpus size, and the overall verdict is stated as 'strong pass on all dimensions with a small corpus'.

nodes.label: Review: rsl-siege-manager worked example
nodes.rationale: A worked-example review dated 2026-05-15 of graphify run on glitchwerks/rsl-siege-manager @ 6085fd66. It evaluates the headline outputs in GRAPH_REPORT.md — god nodes, surprising connections, communities, isolated nodes, suggested questions — and quotes the report verbatim so each finding is verifiable against the committed artifacts.

nodes.label: Single evaluation criterion: would a familiar developer nominate this?
nodes.rationale: The review judges the report's headline outputs against one criterion: do they reflect things a developer familiar with this codebase would themselves nominate as core, surprising, or worth investigating? Every finding quotes the report directly so the judgement is checkable.

nodes.label: Corpus condition of the tests-included run
nodes.rationale: The committed run has tests included and no .graphifyignore, producing 1886 nodes, 3876 edges, 141 communities, and a 90% EXTRACTED / 10% INFERRED split with an average INFERRED confidence of 0.62. Every finding in the review is conditioned on that run configuration.

nodes.label: ~10 minutes of CLI time end-to-end
nodes.rationale: Setup for the reviewed run took roughly ten minutes of CLI time end-to-end.

nodes.label: $0 cost: tree-sitter only, no LLM calls fired
nodes.rationale: The run cost $0 because this corpus's natural file mix surfaced no non-code files in meaningful quantity: tree-sitter handles all 29 supported languages locally, and LLM calls fire only for non-code files.

nodes.label: Throughput: 1886 nodes in a few minutes
nodes.rationale: Listed under what worked well: 1886 nodes were extracted in a few minutes at $0 cost, with local tree-sitter parsing doing the work.

nodes.label: Finding 1 — test fixtures dominate the god-node list
nodes.rationale: With tests included, six of the top ten god nodes (_make_siege 124 edges, _make_member, _make_position, _make_building, _make_group, makeSiegeMember) are test factory functions and a seventh is a test session fixture. The report labels that list 'your core abstractions', yet no developer would nominate _make_siege() as a core abstraction of a siege-assignment web app.

nodes.label: Why degree centrality saturates on test factories
nodes.rationale: The pattern is structural, not corpus-specific: factories create the primary domain objects every test exercises, so they accumulate edges from every part of the suite. The better the test coverage, the more saturated the factory's degree count.

nodes.label: .graphifyignore excluding test directories
nodes.rationale: The documented mitigation — a .graphifyignore excluding tests/, __tests__/ and similar (here backend/tests/ and frontend/src/**/__tests__/) — is effective at removing this class of false-positive god node for users running graphify on well-covered codebases.

nodes.label: Finding 2 — the without-tests god-node list
nodes.rationale: An earlier run of the same corpus with tests ignored produced a god-node list mixing three legitimate domain models with page components, a class-merge utility and document/wiki entities. Those artifacts are not committed — only the tests-included ones are — but the list is reproducible by re-running with the same .graphifyignore.

nodes.label: Legitimate domain models surfaced
nodes.rationale: Three of the ten without-tests god nodes — SiegeMember (55 edges), BuildingType (27) and MemberRole (25) — are legitimate domain models a developer would identify, and the review counts them as a genuine domain extraction that worked.

nodes.label: React page components inflated by entry-point imports
